cards.title: Diagnose the Growth Bottleneck: Traffic/Match vs. Conversion
cards.summary: Separate a low conversion rate into its two causes, wrong traffic or weak offer, before investing in CRO.
cards.use_when: Your store's conversion rate looks low relative to category norms and you are deciding whether to invest in CRO, new creative, or audience targeting.
steps: Pull conversion rate by traffic source and campaign rather than as one blended number, so you can see whether specific sources drag the average down.
Apply the source's diagnostic: a low blended conversion rate is either (a) targeting/traffic mismatch, or (b) genuinely weak onsite conversion. Check which by segmenting.

If specific geographies, placements or audiences convert near zero while others convert normally, treat it as a traffic-mismatch problem and fix targeting first; improving the page will not convert people who were never buyers.

Prioritize better-matched traffic over CRO work when the mismatch is the dominant cause, because, per the source, 'the easiest way to improve your conversion is just get better people' into the funnel.
Only after traffic is reasonably matched should you run CRO tests on PDP, offer and checkout, since CRO cannot fix irrelevant traffic.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion and framing, not a proven rule; both causes can coexist and should be tested, not assumed.
Do not abandon CRO entirely; the point is sequencing when the data shows a clear audience mismatch.

cards.title: Identify the Owner's Core Skill to Locate the Missing Function
cards.summary: Name whether you are product/brand-led or media-buying-led to find which capability the business lacks.
cards.use_when: You are a founder stuck at a revenue plateau and deciding what to hire, learn, or outsource next.
steps: Ask yourself directly which core functions you are genuinely strong at: sourcing/product selection and brand, or media buying and customer acquisition.
In ecommerce, per the source, the two common owner archetypes are (a) product/brand-focused operators and (b) hardcore media buyers; most owners lean clearly to one.
If you have supply/product selection down but cannot immediately say you are strong at media buying, treat media buying as the likely missing capability and hire or learn there first.
Prioritize: drive revenue now with the missing acquisition skill, then build brand once sales volume is higher.
Reassess after the gap is filled; the next missing function (brand, retention, ops) only becomes the bottleneck after the first is solved.
caveats: This is the presenter's situational framework, not a validated model; an owner may be strong or weak in both or neither.
Being 'in the middle' is not a judgment of ability, only a way to locate the deficiency.

cards.title: Use Equity and Non-Cash Levers to Land a Star Media Buyer
cards.summary: When margins are thin, compensate elite acquisition talent with equity or other levers instead of only cash salary.
cards.use_when: Your store is profitable but margins are too thin to pay a top-tier media buyer a full market salary, and you need that capability to scale.
steps: Calculate your real margin (the source example: ~$400k profit on $3M revenue, roughly 12%) to see how much cash compensation you can absorb without erasing profit.
Recognize that top media buyers earn multiple hundreds of thousands of dollars a year, so a full cash salary may consume a large share of thin margins.
Offer a mix: cash, equity points, and other assets you hold such as stock/inventory, to bridge the compensation gap without giving away the entire margin.
Decide consciously between learning media buying yourself or bringing in a 'star' and paying with equity; the source frames this as a real trade-off, not a default.
Verify current compensation norms and equity expectations before making an offer, as these vary by market and time.
caveats: Equity dilutes ownership and must be structured deliberately; the source does not specify vesting or terms.
The dollar figures are from one example brand, not a benchmark for your store.

cards.title: Why Ecommerce Can Scale Fast, and Where the Cash Trap Appears
cards.summary: Ecommerce revenue can scale quickly with the right acquisition person, but growth creates a cash-flow strain to plan for.
cards.use_when: You are forecasting an aggressive growth push (e.g., doubling revenue) and evaluating whether your cash can support it.
steps: Treat rapid revenue scaling as feasible with the right media-buying capability, per the source's framing that ecommerce 'scales very easily'.
Before committing to a growth sprint, model cash flow separately from revenue: faster sales typically means buying more inventory and paying for ads ahead of collecting revenue.
Identify your funding levers - cash reserves and stock/inventory - that can bridge the gap during a growth push.
Plan the cash cycle before scaling, since the source explicitly flags cash flow as the problem that 'comes up' after rapid growth, deferred to be dealt with deliberately.
Sequence: confirm the acquisition capability and cash runway, then push spend.
caveats: The claim that revenue can double 'in like 60 days' is the presenter's opinion, not a promise or typical result.
Cash-flow mechanics depend on your payment terms, inventory lead times and returns; model with your own numbers.

cards.title: Leverage Product Arbitrage as a Durable Moat
cards.summary: A strong sourcing eye for under/over-valued inventory is a core asset that partially substitutes for brand strength.
cards.use_when: You are assessing what actually differentiates your store and deciding how much to lean on sourcing versus acquisition spend.
steps: Identify whether your real edge is sourcing - spotting an item you can buy low and resell at a much higher price (the source example: buy at ~$200, sell at ~$2,000).
If sourcing is your strength, treat it as a defensible advantage and build acquisition and brand on top of it rather than diluting focus.
Note the source's point that unique inventory can create a 'brand halo' - use distinctive, hard-to-source products as a natural differentiator in messaging and merchandising.
Do not assume the sourcing skill alone drives growth; pair it with the missing acquisition capability to convert the advantage into revenue.
caveats: The buy/sell figures are a single example, not a margin rule for your catalog.
Sourcing advantages can erode as competitors find the same supply; brand and retention still matter long-term.

cards.title: Sequence Brand Building After Revenue Growth
cards.summary: Prioritize near-term sales and revenue before investing in becoming a recognized brand, per the source's ordering.
cards.use_when: You are allocating effort between brand-building activities (content, identity, PR) and direct revenue-driving acquisition.
steps: When stuck, the source advises: get more sales and drive revenue up first, then make brand the next focus.
For now, direct resources toward the acquisition capability that produces immediate revenue rather than long-horizon brand work.
Once revenue and the acquisition engine are working, shift to learning how to brand the business for long-term recognition in the category.
Use any existing brand halo from unique products as a short-term asset without over-investing in full brand programs prematurely.
caveats: This is a sequencing opinion, not a universal rule; some businesses with strong differentiation may benefit from brand investment earlier.
Brand and revenue are not strictly sequential; the source presents this as a prioritization, not an absolute.

cards.title: Build the Team Around Proven Strength, Not Assumed Skill
cards.summary: Recognize which function you genuinely own and hire specifically for the gap, not for general 'management'.
cards.use_when: You are planning a headcount addition and unsure which role to prioritize for your next growth phase.
steps: Diagnose which core ecommerce functions - sourcing, media buying, brand - you currently own and evidence with results rather than aspiration.
Scan your own vocabulary for hedges ('I'm not sure', 'I don't know'); the source treats not immediately naming your strength as a signal the skill is missing.
Hire specifically for the missing function. If media buying is the gap, avoid hiring a generalist 'A player' without a defined function; define the role around acquisition.
Confirm the hire's scope against the growth lever you are pulling - in this example, media buying to move from $3M toward higher revenue.
Revisit the org chart after the gap closes to identify the next missing function (e.g., brand, customer success).
caveats: The source does not prescribe a hiring process or vetting method; it frames the diagnostic only.
Avoid over-reading hesitation; a founder may simply be modest about a skill they actually have.

cards.title: Prioritize the Actual Bottleneck Over the Assumed One
cards.summary: When stuck at a plateau, verify whether your constraint is leads/traffic, conversion, or something else before acting.
cards.use_when: Your store has plateaued and you are deciding whether to fix traffic, conversion, or a different function.
steps: Start by stating the explicit constraint: e.g., 'leads and converting leads' splits into two distinct problems - getting people onto the site, and converting them once there.
Distinguish lead volume from conversion rate clearly; in the example a ~1% conversion rate was flagged as possibly low, but the presenter tied it to traffic quality as an alternative cause.
Use the source's diagnostic question: are you actually good at the core function that presumably limits growth (here, media buying)? An unclear answer suggests that is the bottleneck.
Avoid defaulting to CRO obsession; the source argues improving traffic quality can be the more overlooked and easier conversion lever.
Then allocate effort to the identified bottleneck rather than the one that feels most familiar.
caveats: The ~1% conversion rate observation is context-specific and should be compared to your own category and source mix, not adopted as a benchmark.
The presenter is offering a hypothesis about this one business; validate with your own funnel data.
